Tachysurus nitidus (Sauvage & Dabry de Thiersant, 1874). Family Bagridae. Type locality: Chang Jiang [Yangtze River], China. IUCN Red List category: Not Evaluated.

Tachysurus can be identified by an extrascapular without a laterosensory canal, and a pterotic with a broad lateral laminar expansion. It is among the most speciose catfish groups in East Asia and its members inhabit habitats ranging from fast-flowing hillstreams to large rivers.
Asia: Yangtze-Kiang, China. Reported from South Korea.

Asia: China, from Heilongjiang (Amur River) to Minjiang (Yangtze River tributary). Type locality: Yang-tze-kiang, China.

IUCN Red List: Tachysurus nitidus is a freshwater catfish species that is broadly distributed throughout China and the Korean Peninsula, occurring in artificial reservoirs, lakes, small hill streams, and rivers. This species often comprises a dominant portion of ichthyofauna in China, but appears to be less common on the Korean Peninsula. There is currently no indication that the global population is in decline, despite a continuing inferred decline in habitat quality resulting from several regionally pervasive threats. Given a broad distribution and lack of evidence of decline, T. nitidus is assessed as Least Concern (IUCN 2023).
Males have an elongate genital papilla in front of the anal fin.

Currently treated in some publications, and FishBase (2009), as Pelteobagrus nitidus. Was named as Leiocassis nitidus before this. Still found in some online sources as Pseudobagrus nitidus.

Etymology: The genus name Tachysurus: tachys, swift; oura, tail, referring to the presumed agility of T. sinensis based on its "long and nimble" tail (translation). The specific name nitidus: neat, elegant or shining, allusion not explained, perhaps referring to "reddish body, wine-coloured towards the back" (translation).
Annales des Sciences Naturelles, Paris (Zoologie et Paléontologie) (Sér. 6) v. 1 (art. 5), pp 5.
